subject: EVS
title: Water — The Essence of Life
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 1, Water — The Essence of Life, the topics are: Saltwater and Freshwater, water has different forms, water cycle, groundwater, surface water, life in water — animals, kinds of plants in water. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Saltwater and Freshwater
Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water
Water has Different Forms
Water exists as solid (ice, snow), liquid (rain) and vapour (steam)
Water Cycle
The Sun's heat turns water into vapour, the vapour forms clouds, and water falls back as rain, snow or hail into rivers, lakes ...
Groundwater
Some rainwater soaks into the soil and sinks through soil and rocks; the water stored deep underground is groundwater
Surface Water
Rivers, ponds and lakes are surface freshwater
Life in Water — Animals
Animals in and around water have special features — fins to swim, webbed feet, long legs, special mouths — and they depend on ...
Types of Plants in Water
Water plants float freely, float with roots in the pond bed, stay under water, or grow at the edges

items: Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water. Only a little is freshwater — and every living being needs it to live.
Most of Earth's water is salty
Freshwater is very little
Without water, life would not be possible
Water exists as solid (ice, snow), liquid (rain) and vapour (steam). Heating and cooling change one form into another and back again.
Three forms: solid, liquid, vapour
Heating: ice → water → vapour
Cooling: vapour → water → ice
Water can change into ice and steam and return to liquid
The Sun's heat turns water into vapour, the vapour forms clouds, and water falls back as rain, snow or hail into rivers, lakes and oceans — again and again.
Heat → vapour → clouds → rain/snow/hail → rivers, lakes, oceans
The same water goes round again and again
Some rainwater soaks into the soil and sinks through soil and rocks; the water stored deep underground is groundwater. Open ground lets it recharge; cement stops it.
Groundwater = water stored deep underground
Wells, borewells, tube wells, handpumps draw it
Open ground recharges it; cement stops it
Rivers, ponds and lakes are surface freshwater. A river starts high in the mountains and flows down; water flows, stops or curves by the shape of the land, and flowing water also changes the land.
Water flows from higher to lower ground
Water flows, stops or curves by the shape of the land
Flowing water can change the shape of land
Some rivers reach the Bay of Bengal, some the Arabian Sea
Animals in and around water have special features — fins to swim, webbed feet, long legs, special mouths — and they depend on water and on each other for food.
Fins, webbed feet, long legs suit life in or near water
Animals depend on each other for food
Many living beings live near water bodies
Water plants float freely, float with roots in the pond bed, stay under water, or grow at the edges. Waxy, waterproof leaves and long roots help them live in water.
Four kinds: floating, rooted floating, under water, edge
Waxy coating keeps leaves waterproof and healthy
Freshwater supports a rich variety of life
Wrong: There is so much water on Earth that we can never run short of drinking water. Right: Most of it is salty; freshwater is only like a teaspoon in a glass
Wrong: The droplets outside the cold glass leak out from inside. Right: Steel has no holes; the droplets come from water vapour in the air that cools on the cold glass
Wrong: Clouds are made of smoke or cotton. Right: The book says water vapour forms the clouds — clouds are water, not smoke
Wrong: Groundwater is a big river flowing under the ground. Right: It is water stored in the gaps of soil and rock layers deep underground
Wrong: Rivers flow in straight lines. Right: They curve and spread by the shape of the land, like the mustard seeds
Wrong: Every animal at a pond lives inside the water. Right: Some, like the pond heron and dragonfly, live around the water and depend on it

sol_items: Where does rainwater come from, and where does it : It comes from clouds made of water vapour. It falls into rivers, lakes and oceans or soaks into the ground.
Can we drink ocean water?: No. It is salty and not fit for drinking.
What can ocean water be used for?: Making salt, travel by ships, fishing, and as a home for sea life.
Identify freshwater sources in the pictures: Rivers, lakes, ponds, wells and rain are freshwater (read from the pictures).
Is there water in air? Is snow a form of water?: Yes, there is water vapour in air. Yes, snow is frozen water.
Where do droplets on a cold glass come from?: From water vapour in the air that cools and turns to water on the cold glass.
imp_items: Which kind of water is most on Earth?
Salty ocean water
Name the three forms of water with one example each.
Solid: ice; liquid: rain; vapour: steam
Why do drops form outside a cold glass?
Water vapour in the air cools on the glass and turns into water drops
What are clouds made of?
Water vapour and tiny droplets
What is groundwater? Name two ways we get it.
Water stored deep under the ground; wells and handpumps
Why does a green lawn help recharge groundwater but a cement floor does not?
Water soaks into soil but cannot pass through cement

subject: EVS
title: Journey of a River
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 2, Journey of a River, the topics are: Journey of a River — From Source to Sea, the life a river holds — perennial and seasonal rivers, how a river supports lives, dams — storing water, changing the flow, river pollution — what pollutes a river and why it matters, when a river floods — causes and effects, flood safety — before, during and after a flood, when a river runs dry — water shortage and saving water. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Journey of a River — From Source to Sea
A river begins as a small stream at its source and grows wider as rainwater and tributaries join it
The Life a River Holds — Perennial and Seasonal Rivers
Godavari flows all year (perennial); some rivers flow only in the rainy season (seasonal)
How a River Supports Lives
People have lived near rivers since ancient times
Dams — Storing Water, Changing the Flow
A dam is a giant wall that blocks a river and stores its water in a reservoir for dry seasons; but the stored water floods land, ...
River Pollution — What Pollutes a River and Why It Matters
Waste, plastic, dirty soapy water, chemicals and fertilisers pollute a river; people who use it can fall sick and animals ...
When a River Floods — Causes and Effects
Too much rain makes a river faster, deeper and bigger until it overflows its banks and floods houses, fields and roads
Flood Safety — Before, During and After a Flood
Staying safe in a flood means getting ready before it comes, moving to higher ground and staying out of flood water during it, ...
When a River Runs Dry — Water Shortage and Saving Water
When there is no water for a long time, families may have to leave their homes and animals suffer

notes.h: Journey of a River — From Source to Sea
items: A river begins as a small stream at its source and grows wider as rainwater and tributaries join it. Godavari flows across many states and spreads into a delta where it meets the sea.
Godavari: source → tributaries → states → delta
Godavari: Trimbakeshwar to Bay of Bengal, 1,465 km, second longest after Ganga

notes.h: The Life a River Holds — Perennial and Seasonal Rivers
items: Godavari flows all year (perennial); some rivers flow only in the rainy season (seasonal). A river and its forests and delta are home to many plants and animals.
Perennial = flows all year; seasonal = only in the rainy season
A river is home to many plants and animals

People have lived near rivers since ancient times. A river gives water for drinking, cooking, washing, farming and factories, carried in pipes and canals; it gives livelihoods and is part of people's faith and festivals.
Water it gives: daily needs, farming, factories
Life around it: homes, livelihoods, faith and festivals

notes.h: Dams — Storing Water, Changing the Flow
items: A dam is a giant wall that blocks a river and stores its water in a reservoir for dry seasons; but the stored water floods land, and people and animals living there must move.
Dam = giant wall; reservoir = stored water
Gives water and electricity; floods land and moves people and animals

notes.h: River Pollution — What Pollutes a River and Why It Matters
items: Waste, plastic, dirty soapy water, chemicals and fertilisers pollute a river; people who use it can fall sick and animals disappear. Harmful things can hide even in clear water. Making less waste and keeping waste out helps.
Polluters: waste, plastic, soapy water, chemicals, fertilisers
Clear is not always clean
Make less waste; keep waste out of water

notes.h: When a River Floods — Causes and Effects
items: Too much rain makes a river faster, deeper and bigger until it overflows its banks and floods houses, fields and roads. Without trees the water runs off faster; trees slow it and help the soil soak it up.
Too much rain → river overflows its banks → flood
Trees slow rain water; no trees → faster run-off → more flooding

notes.h: Flood Safety — Before, During and After a Flood
items: Staying safe in a flood means getting ready before it comes, moving to higher ground and staying out of flood water during it, and waiting until it is declared safe after it.
Before: get ready; During: go higher, stay out of water; After: wait till declared safe
Keep an emergency kit ready

notes.h: When a River Runs Dry — Water Shortage and Saving Water
items: When there is no water for a long time, families may have to leave their homes and animals suffer. Water ATMs, the National Water Mission and our own small daily actions help use water wisely.
No water for long → people move, animals suffer
Water ATMs, National Water Mission
Tap off, fix leaks, reuse clean water
Wrong: A river is big right from where it begins. Right: It starts as a small stream and grows as rainwater and tributaries join it
Wrong: Every river has water all year. Right: Seasonal rivers flow only when they get rain water; only perennial rivers flow all year
Wrong: Tap water is made in the tap or the tank. Right: It travels from a river, dam or other source through pipes
Wrong: A dam only helps and never harms anyone. Right: Its reservoir floods land; animals and people living there have to move
Wrong: If river water looks clear, it is clean and safe. Right: Dissolved chemicals and soapy water cannot be seen — clear is not always clean
Wrong: Floods are only nature's doing; people have nothing to do with them. Right: Cutting trees lets rain water run off faster and makes flooding worse

sol_items: Name the states Godavari flows through: Read from the map: Maharashtra, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Puducherry (Yanam).
Which small rivers join the Godavari?: Tributaries such as Manjira, Pranhita and Indravati (read from the map).
Why did people build homes near rivers?: They need water to drink and farm, and rivers give food and easy travel.
What happens when a dam is built? Problems and sol: Water is stored but land floods; people and animals must move. Plan new homes and protect wildlife.
Where do plastic wrappers we litter end up?: In drains, then rivers and seas, where they harm animals.
Things thrown in the bin and harm if thrown into a: Plastic chokes animals; chemicals poison water; food waste rots and smells.
imp_items: What is a tributary?
A small river that joins a bigger river
What is a delta?
Where a river spreads into many streams near the sea
Differentiate perennial and seasonal rivers.
Perennial flows all year; seasonal flows only in the rainy season
What is a dam and a reservoir?
A dam is a giant wall across a river; a reservoir is the water stored behind it
Give two benefits and one problem of a dam.
Stores water and gives electricity; floods land and people move
Why is clear water not always clean?
Chemicals and soap dissolved in water cannot be seen

subject: EVS
title: The Mystery of Food
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 3, The Mystery of Food, the topics are: Food Spoilage — What Spoils Food?, good microbes — idli, curd and digestion, why some foods spoil faster — what microbes need, drying and dehydration, pickling, oiling and airtight packing, refrigeration and freezing, salt, sugar and spices, my food, my pride — fresh, local and seasonal food, teeth and chewing, oral hygiene. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Food Spoilage — What Spoils Food?
Food spoils when tiny living things called microbes grow on it
Good Microbes — Idli, Curd and Digestion
Not all microbes are bad
Why Some Foods Spoil Faster — What Microbes Need
Microbes need moisture, air and the right temperature to grow
Drying and Dehydration
Drying in the Sun removes moisture from food
Pickling, Oiling and Airtight Packing
Oil poured over a pickle keeps out air, so microbes cannot grow
Refrigeration and Freezing
A fridge makes the temperature too cold for microbes to grow — cold slows them down
Salt, Sugar and Spices
Since long ago people have used salt, sugar and spices like pepper to keep food from spoiling — and we still do
My Food, My Pride — Fresh, Local and Seasonal Food
Food traditions pass from one generation to the next
Teeth and Chewing
Chewing breaks food into small pieces and then mush, and releases saliva that helps digestion
Oral Hygiene
Oral hygiene means keeping the mouth and teeth clean: rinse after eating, brush regularly and eat fewer sweets

items: Food spoils when tiny living things called microbes grow on it. Spoiled food smells bad and shows coloured patches of mould — a colony of thousands of microbes.
Microbes are found in soil, water, the air around us, in plants, animals and inside us (Finding #1)
Microbes change the taste and smell of food

notes.h: Good Microbes — Idli, Curd and Digestion
items: Not all microbes are bad. Microbes in the air help idli batter rise; microbes in curd join the good microbes in our stomach and help digestion.
Some microbes spoil our food while some help us make food items and digest food (Final Discovery)
Sometimes bad eating habits can also lead to indigestion (Finding #8)

notes.h: Why Some Foods Spoil Faster — What Microbes Need
items: Microbes need moisture, air and the right temperature to grow. Food that gives them these spoils fast; take away any one and microbes stop.
Microbes need moisture, air and the right temperature to grow
All life needs water and air to survive
If we remove any one of these, we can stop microbes in their tracks
Finding #2: keep air and water away from the microbes
Drying in the Sun removes moisture from food. Without moisture microbes cannot grow, so dried food lasts the whole year.
Finding #3: drying in the Sun removes the moisture from the chillies — without moisture, microbes cannot grow
Oil poured over a pickle keeps out air, so microbes cannot grow. Food factories do the same with airtight cans and packaging.
Finding #4: oil keeps out air and stops the growth of microbes
In food factories, food is preserved in airtight cans and packaging to keep microbes away
A fridge makes the temperature too cold for microbes to grow — cold slows them down. Butter needs the fridge, but ghee, which is butter with its water removed by heating, does not.
Fridges make the temperature too cold for microbes to grow
Finding #5: cold temperature slows down microbes
Since long ago people have used salt, sugar and spices like pepper to keep food from spoiling — and we still do. Every family has its own ways to preserve food.
Finding #6: there are many ways in which food is being preserved

notes.h: My Food, My Pride — Fresh, Local and Seasonal Food
items: Food traditions pass from one generation to the next. Elders check fruits and vegetables carefully before buying, and seasonal, local fruits are fresh and taste best.
Many traditional practices about food are passed on from one generation to another in the family
Finding #9: fruits taste best when they are eaten in their season; waiting for them increases the joy

Chewing breaks food into small pieces and then mush, and releases saliva that helps digestion. Four kinds of teeth do four jobs: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars crush, molars grind. Chewing properly and eating slowly also keep us from choking.
Finding #10: chewing food properly breaks down the food and releases saliva which helps in digestion
Finding #11: different kinds of teeth have different uses
Finding #13: I must eat my food slowly to avoid choking on it
Oral hygiene means keeping the mouth and teeth clean: rinse after eating, brush regularly and eat fewer sweets. A cavity is a hole in a tooth; a dentist treats it and also gives check-ups.
Wrong: Microbes are like little lice — we can see them with our eyes. Right: They are much smaller; we need a microscope. We see mould only because thousands of microbes grow together
Wrong: All microbes make food bad or make us ill. Right: Good microbes make idli batter rise, make curd and help digestion

Wrong: Food spoils just because it becomes old. Right: Food spoils because microbes grow on it; if they cannot get moisture, air or the right temperature, food lasts long — like the 2-month-old pickle
Wrong: Only chillies can be dried. Right: Many foods are dried: tomatoes, mangoes, papad, roti (khakhra), fish
Wrong: Oil is added to pickle only for taste. Right: Oil stops air from getting in, which keeps the pickle safe from microbes
Wrong: The fridge kills all microbes, so food lasts forever inside it. Right: Cold only slows microbes down — food in the fridge also spoils after some time

sol_items: Why does food spoil?: Microbes grow on it and change its smell and taste.
What else is dried to last all year?: Tomatoes, mangoes, papad, fish, peas and chillies.
Items made from mangoes to last longer: Aam papad, pickle, jam and dried slices.
Tomato slices in sunlight; how to preserve tomato: They lose water and shrink. Dried tomatoes keep for a long time.
What if no oil were added to the pickle?: Air would reach it and microbes would grow, so it would spoil.
Why does butter need a fridge but ghee does not?: Butter has water that lets microbes grow; ghee has no water because heating removes it.
imp_items: What are microbes?
Very tiny living things seen only with a microscope
What is mould?
Coloured patches on food; a colony of thousands of microbes
Name two uses of good microbes.
Make idli batter rise and curd; help digestion
What three things do microbes need?
Moisture, air and the right temperature
How does drying keep food safe?
It removes moisture so microbes cannot grow
Why is oil poured over pickle?
Oil keeps out air so microbes cannot grow

subject: EVS
title: Our School — A Happy Place
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 4, Our School — A Happy Place, the topics are: Green School, be a school explorer!, waste management, let us be cool!, dripping water, greenery around us, traffic signs, fire safety, what we do matters!. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Green School
School is a happy place where we feel safe and cared for and learn every day
Be a School Explorer!
Before changing anything we look closely at our school: we draw a map, form explorer teams that each observe one thing, and then ...
Waste Management
We reduce waste by using only what we need and reusing things
Let Us be Cool!
Shade from trees, windows that let the breeze in, and a white roof keep rooms cool
Dripping Water
Water is a precious treasure
Greenery Around Us
Trees are home to many living beings
Traffic Signs
Many road accidents happen because people do not follow traffic rules correctly
Fire Safety
Fires do not happen often, but being prepared helps everyone feel safer and more confident: know where the fire extinguisher and ...
What We do Matters!
Our behaviour can make a place peaceful and welcoming or uncomfortable and unpleasant

items: School is a happy place where we feel safe and cared for and learn every day. A green school manages its waste, saves water, uses electricity carefully and keeps its campus green by planting and caring for trees.
School is a happy place — safe, caring, full of learning
Green school = manage waste, save water, use electricity carefully, keep the campus green
Every child has the right to a clean and safe school
If there is a difficulty at school, tell a teacher, the principal or your parents
Before changing anything we look closely at our school: we draw a map, form explorer teams that each observe one thing, and then share what we found.
Each group decides what to observe before exploring
After exploring, share: what did you find, what worried you, what surprised you, what made you proud

We reduce waste by using only what we need and reusing things. What still remains is separated: wet waste in the green bin, dry waste in the blue bin, and useful items like old newspapers go to recyclers.
Reduce and reuse first; separating waste into dry and wet helps manage it better and keeps our surroundings clean (p. 59)
Separate: wet → green bin, dry → blue bin, useful items → recycler
If waste is not separated, it gets dirty and smelly, useful things cannot be recycled, and sanitation workers' work becomes harder and less safe (added)
Recyclers and sanitation workers do important work — respect them
Shade from trees, windows that let the breeze in, and a white roof keep rooms cool. A white surface reflects the Sun's heat while a black surface absorbs it.
Shade, breeze and a white roof keep rooms cool
White reflects heat, black absorbs heat
Cooling without electricity saves electricity
Water is a precious treasure. Even a small leak wastes a lot of water over time, so we fix leaks, use water carefully and collect rainwater.
Water is a precious treasure
Small drips add up to a lot of water
Fix leaks, use water wisely, collect rainwater
Trees are home to many living beings. They keep the air clean, give shade, give food to birds and insects, and keep the surroundings cool.
Trees are home to many living beings
They keep the air clean
They give shade
They give food to birds and insects
Many road accidents happen because people do not follow traffic rules correctly. We must know the rules, follow them, and help make the school gate safer.
Many accidents happen because traffic rules are not followed
Know the rules and follow them
A clear sign helps drivers, parents and students
Fires do not happen often, but being prepared helps everyone feel safer and more confident: know where the fire extinguisher and the assembly point are, and practise a calm fire drill.
Know where the fire extinguisher is
Know your assembly point
Move calmly, crawl low under smoke, never hide, never go back, tell a teacher who is missing

Our behaviour can make a place peaceful and welcoming or uncomfortable and unpleasant. We show respect and kindness by waiting for our turn, using kind words, helping someone and keeping our place clean.
Behaviour makes a place peaceful or unpleasant
Wait for your turn, use kind words, help someone, keep places clean
When we are kind and polite, everyone feels happy
Wrong: A green school is a school painted green. Right: A green school manages waste, saves water, uses electricity carefully and keeps the campus green with trees
Wrong: Exploring means just walking around the school. Right: Each team first decides what to observe, then looks carefully and notes what it finds
Wrong: All waste can go into one bin. Right: Separate it — wet waste in the green bin, dry waste in the blue bin, useful items to recyclers
Wrong: A black roof keeps a house cooler. Right: Black absorbs the Sun's heat and gets hot; white reflects it and stays cool
Wrong: A few drops from a tap don't matter. Right: Drop by drop, a small leak can fill many glasses in one day
Wrong: Trees only give us shade. Right: They are also homes, give food to birds and insects, keep the air clean and keep the place cool

sol_items: Colour of the bin for dry and wet waste: Dry waste: blue bin. Wet waste: green bin.
Things given to recyclers by school and by parents: Old newspapers, bottles and cartons.
What if we do not separate waste?: Useful things are wasted and sanitation workers find it hard and unsafe.
How can we make sanitation workers' work easier?: Separate waste, close bins and say thank you.
Black tile and white tile in the Sun: The white tile felt cooler because it reflects heat; black absorbs it.
A white roof; keeping an area cool: The rooms below stay cooler. Plant trees, keep windows open and use white roofs.
imp_items: What is a green school?
A school that manages waste, saves water and power and plants trees
Which bin is for wet waste?
Green bin
Why must we separate waste?
Useful things can be reused and sanitation workers are safe
Name three things that go to recyclers.
Newspaper, plastic bottles and tins
Why does a white roof keep rooms cool?
White reflects the Sun heat
Give three ways to keep a room cool.
Shade trees, open windows and a white roof

subject: EVS
title: Our Vibrant Country
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 5, Our Vibrant Country, the topics are: Republic Day in Our School, why we celebrate republic day, india in our currency note, national symbols of india, many languages of india, diversity everywhere: headgear of india, music and dance of india, spirit of togetherness. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Republic Day in Our School
On 26 January, Republic Day, the whole school gathers at the flagpole, the tricolour is unfurled and we sing the National Anthem ...
Why We Celebrate Republic Day
India became free on 15 August 1947 (Independence Day)
India in Our Currency Note
A currency note is a small picture of India: it shows many languages, two images of Gandhi ji, the Swachh Bharat spectacles, a ...
National Symbols of India
National symbols — like the National Emblem, the national animal (tiger) and the national bird (peacock) — remind us who we are ...
Many Languages of India
More than a thousand languages are spoken in India, each rich with its own history, songs and stories; the same thing, like a ...
Diversity Everywhere: Headgear of India
Like a forest with many kinds of plants and animals, diversity makes India stronger
Music and Dance of India
Music and dance are art forms for celebrating, praying, sharing stories and bringing people together; even a drum looks and ...
Spirit of Togetherness
India's many languages, religions, clothes and traditions are like threads woven into one strong, colourful fabric; we live ...

items: On 26 January, Republic Day, the whole school gathers at the flagpole, the tricolour is unfurled and we sing the National Anthem together with pride; every colour of the flag stands for something.
Republic Day is on 26 January
The tricolour is unfurled and the National Anthem is sung together
Saffron — strength, courage; white — peace, truth; chakra — duty; green — growth, prosperity

India became free on 15 August 1947 (Independence Day). A free country needs rules, so on 26 January 1950 India began to follow its book of rules, the Constitution — that is why 26 January is Republic Day, celebrated with a grand parade in New Delhi.
15 August 1947 — Independence Day
26 January 1950 — we began to follow the Constitution
Republic Day parade in New Delhi: jets, tableaux, cultural programmes, Defence Forces

A currency note is a small picture of India: it shows many languages, two images of Gandhi ji, the Swachh Bharat spectacles, a monument from a state, symbols and special help for people who cannot see.
Two images of Gandhi ji — hold the note to the light
Spectacles = Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (Clean India Mission)
₹10 — Sun Temple of Konark, Odisha
Raised prints and the MANI app help people with visual impairment

National symbols — like the National Emblem, the national animal (tiger) and the national bird (peacock) — remind us who we are and make us proud to be Indians; states and even schools can have their own symbols.
Emblem: three lions — strength, courage, confidence; Ashoka Chakra below
Tiger — national animal; peacock — national bird
Lions in the wild: only in Gir, Gujarat — saved from a few dozen to several hundred
More than a thousand languages are spoken in India, each rich with its own history, songs and stories; the same thing, like a mango, has a different name in each language.
More than 1000 languages in India
Each language has its own history, songs and stories
Translation apps help us understand other languages

Like a forest with many kinds of plants and animals, diversity makes India stronger. Headgear shows it: it differs from state to state and tells where someone is from, what they believe and what they do — and some headgear protects us.
Diversity makes a forest — and a country — stronger
Saafa/pagri — Rajasthan; topi — Himachal Pradesh
Helmets are compulsory on two-wheelers

Music and dance are art forms for celebrating, praying, sharing stories and bringing people together; even a drum looks and sounds different in each part of India, and dance forms come from different states.
Music and dance help us celebrate, pray, share stories and come together
11 drums in the book — tabla, dhol, mridangam …
Mridangam — Carnatic; sitar, shehnai — Hindustani

India's many languages, religions, clothes and traditions are like threads woven into one strong, colourful fabric; we live together helping each other, keep our rich past and add new colours of the future — and as proud citizens we care for our country.
Kinds of diversity: language, headgear and clothes, food, music, dance
Many threads, one strong fabric
Rich past (ayurveda, yoga, meditation) + exciting future
Proud citizens care for their country

Wrong: The colours of the flag are only for decoration. Right: Each colour stands for something: saffron strength and courage, white peace and truth, green growth and prosperity; the chakra stands for duty
Wrong: India became free on 26 January. Right: India became free on 15 August 1947; on 26 January 1950 it began to follow its Constitution
Wrong: There is only one picture of Gandhi ji on a note. Right: There are two — a smaller one is seen when the note is held up to the light
Wrong: The lion is India's national animal. Right: The tiger is the national animal; lions are on the National Emblem
Wrong: Everyone in India speaks the same language. Right: More than a thousand languages are spoken across India
Wrong: A neat garden with one kind of plant is stronger than a forest. Right: A forest with many kinds looks after itself and grows stronger — like a diverse country

sol_items: Rivers and mountains named in the National Anthem: Read from the table: Yamuna, Ganga, Vindhya, Himachal (read from the book).
Riddles: orange with black stripes; green and blue feat...: Tiger (national animal); peacock (national bird).
Musical instruments; make one: Sitar, tabla, flute, dholak; a rubber-band guitar from a box (sample).
Monuments on currency notes and their states: Read from the notes: for example Red Fort on the 500 rupee note (Delhi); other monuments from the book table.
India's currency symbol; another country's symbol: The rupee symbol is ₹. Another: $ for the US dollar.
Animals on a ten rupee note: Read from the note (elephant and others).
imp_items: When is Republic Day?
26 January
Why do we celebrate Republic Day?
India began to follow its Constitution on 26 January 1950
When did India become free?
15 August 1947
Name our national animal and bird.
Tiger and peacock
Why do we have national symbols?
They remind us who we are
How many languages are spoken in India?
More than a thousand

subject: EVS
title: Some Unique Places
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 6, Some Unique Places, the topics are: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, life under the sea, sundarbans: home of the mangroves, northeast india: green hills and great traditions, western ghats, nature's hotspot, people living in harmony with nature, protecting unique places. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Andaman and Nicobar Islands
An island is land surrounded by water on all sides
Life Under the Sea
The sea is full of life
Sundarbans: Home of the Mangroves
The Sundarbans, where the Ganga meets the sea, is the largest mangrove forest in the world
Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
Northeast India — the Seven Sisters and Sikkim — is a land of green hills, forests, rivers and wildlife, where weaving, crafts, ...
Western Ghats
The Western Ghats is a long chain of forested hills in western India, passing through six states
Nature's Hotspot
A nature's hotspot is a special place where many plants and animals are found that are not found anywhere else in the world — ...
People Living in Harmony with Nature
In every unique place people depend on nature and care for it in their own way — they use it for food, medicine and their needs, ...
Protecting Unique Places
Unique places and their rare plants and animals must be protected: the government keeps protected areas safe, and people acting ...

items: An island is land surrounded by water on all sides. India's southernmost tip, Indira Point, is in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands — a long chain of islands with unique forests and trees.
Island = land with water on all sides
Indira Point = southernmost tip of India
Capital: Sri Vijaya Puram
Wide roots help island trees stand upright
The sea is full of life. Tiny living corals form colourful reefs that give shelter and homes to fish and many sea creatures, and sea life is important for the whole Earth.
Corals are living animals
Reefs = homes and shelter for sea creatures
Each sea animal has a special feature
Sea life matters for the whole Earth

The Sundarbans, where the Ganga meets the sea, is the largest mangrove forest in the world. Mangroves grow in wet, muddy, salty land; their roots help them breathe and hold the soil against the waves.
Sundarbans = largest mangrove forest
Ganga meets the sea; muddy, salty land
Roots breathe and hold the soil
Mud + Salt + Breathing roots

notes.h: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
items: Northeast India — the Seven Sisters and Sikkim — is a land of green hills, forests, rivers and wildlife, where weaving, crafts, music, dance and festivals are connected to nature, and tree roots grow into living bridges.
Seven Sisters: AA MMM NT, plus Sikkim
Culture and nature grow together
Living root bridges grow from roots
Bhut Jolokia keeps elephants away

The Western Ghats is a long chain of forested hills in western India, passing through six states. Many rivers begin here, and it is rich in plants (many used as medicine) and animals like the lion-tailed macaque.
Long chain of forested hills, six states
Rivers begin here
Lion-tailed macaque found only here
Medicinal plants; 200+ mango kinds

A nature's hotspot is a special place where many plants and animals are found that are not found anywhere else in the world — like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Northeast India and the Western Ghats.
Hotspot = many living things found ONLY here
Hotspots of India: Andaman and Nicobar, Northeast, Western Ghats
Lose them here = lose them from the world, so protect them

notes.h: People Living in Harmony with Nature
items: In every unique place people depend on nature and care for it in their own way — they use it for food, medicine and their needs, read its signs to stay safe, and farm and make crafts without harming it.
People everywhere depend on nature and care for it in their own way
Three ways: Depend on nature, Notice its signs, Create with nature (farming and crafts)
Compare your own region with the places of the journey
Unique places and their rare plants and animals must be protected: the government keeps protected areas safe, and people acting together saved the Silent Valley and are saving the Hargila.
Protect by the Government (protected areas) and by People acting together (Silent Valley, Hargila)
Everything in nature is connected
Islands, forests and hills need our care and respect — learn, respect, protect
Wrong: Kanyakumari is the southernmost tip of India. Right: Indira Point (on an island) is; Kanyakumari is the southernmost point of the mainland
Wrong: Corals are coloured stones or plants. Right: Corals are tiny living sea animals
Wrong: Mangroves are ordinary trees that grow anywhere. Right: They are special trees that grow in wet, salty land
Wrong: Northeast India is only the seven sister states. Right: The Seven Sisters along with Sikkim make up Northeast India
Wrong: The Western Ghats is one single mountain. Right: It is a long chain of forested hills through six states
Wrong: A hotspot is a very hot place. Right: It is a place rich in plants and animals found nowhere else

sol_items: Find India's southernmost point; sea of the Andaman and...: Indira Point, in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. These islands lie in the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea.
Other islands you know: Lakshadweep, Majuli, Sri Lanka and Maldives.
Why are some birds and animals found only on the i: Islands are cut off by sea, so living things grew apart from those elsewhere.
Why is life under the sea as important as in fores: It gives food, oxygen and homes to many living things.
How does a coral reef help sea creatures?: It gives shelter and food and homes to fish and others.
How could knowledge have helped North Sentinel islander...: Knowing the signs of danger such as sea waves would help them move to high land.
imp_items: What is an island?
Land surrounded by water on all sides
Where is Indira Point?
In the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
What is a coral reef?
A colourful home made by tiny living corals
How does a coral reef help sea creatures?
It gives shelter and food
Where are the Sundarbans?
Where the Ganga meets the sea
What is special about mangrove trees?
They grow in salty water and have roots that rise above the mud

subject: EVS
title: Energy — How Things Work
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 7, Energy — How Things Work, the topics are: What Energy Does, food — energy for living things, energy from fuel, electricity, energy from the sun, wind and water, using energy wisely. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: What Energy Does
Energy is what makes things move, light up, make a sound, do work and get warmer or cooler
Food — Energy for Living Things
Food gives humans and animals the energy to move, play, fly and even think
Energy from Fuel
Fuels such as petrol, diesel, cooking gas, wood, coal and oil are burnt to give energy for vehicles, cooking and lamps
Electricity
Electricity runs fans, bulbs and machines — it can give movement, sound, light, heat and cooling
Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
The Sun, the wind and flowing water are natural sources of energy
Using Energy Wisely
Use energy wisely: choose clean sources instead of coal, and save energy — use efficient things like LED bulbs, and live in homes ...

items: Energy is what makes things move, light up, make a sound, do work and get warmer or cooler. We know energy by what it does.
We know energy by what it does: movement, sound, light, change in temperature
Moving air can push things
Vibrating things make sound
Sunlight gives heat
Food gives humans and animals the energy to move, play, fly and even think. The body stores some energy for later.
Food is a source of energy for all living things
Animals get energy from food too
The body stores energy; batteries store energy
Fuels such as petrol, diesel, cooking gas, wood, coal and oil are burnt to give energy for vehicles, cooking and lamps. Burning wood and coal makes smoke and pollution.
Fuel is to vehicles what food is to us
Fuels: petrol, diesel, cooking gas, wood, coal, oil
Wood and coal make smoke — use carefully

Electricity runs fans, bulbs and machines — it can give movement, sound, light, heat and cooling. It makes life easy but is dangerous if used carelessly, and most of it is made by burning coal, which pollutes the air.
Electricity gives movement, sound, light, heat and cooling
Industries and even vehicles use it
Useful but dangerous — follow the safety rules
Mostly made by burning coal → pollution

notes.h: Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
items: The Sun, the wind and flowing water are natural sources of energy. We use them directly (drying clothes, sails, water wheels) and to make electricity (solar panels, windmills, rivers). Electricity made this way is called clean energy.
Sun, wind and flowing water are natural sources of energy
Used directly or to make electricity
Electricity from them is clean energy — no smoke
Use energy wisely: choose clean sources instead of coal, and save energy — use efficient things like LED bulbs, and live in homes that use sunlight and air.
Choose clean sources over coal
Efficiency = same work, less energy (LED)
Homes and nature can save energy
Wrong: Energy means only electricity. Right: Anything that makes things move, sound, light up or change temperature uses energy — rushing air, a plucked band and sunlight too
Wrong: We use energy only when we move or play. Right: Even when we sit, sleep or think, the brain uses energy
Wrong: The cotton wick is the fuel of a diya. Right: The oil is the fuel; the wick alone burns out quickly (added: the wick only carries oil to the flame)
Wrong: Electricity is safe to touch because it stays inside the wires. Right: Plugged-in wires, broken wires and sockets can give a dangerous shock — never touch, always tell an adult
Wrong: We can use the Sun's energy only with a solar panel. Right: Drying clothes and papads uses the Sun's energy directly, without plugging anything
Wrong: Saving energy means doing less work. Right: Energy efficiency means doing the SAME work with less energy — an LED bulb gives the same light with less electricity

sol_items: Things that move, give light, make sound, make coo: Move: fan; light: bulb; sound: bell; cool: fridge; hot: stove.
What makes them move, shine, sound or heat?: Energy such as electricity or fuel.
Do thin and thick rubber bands sound different?: Yes; thin bands make a higher sound, thick a lower sound.
Touch the water in both cups: One is hot and one cold; heat and cold show energy at work.
How do you move? Why tired when hungry?: Food gives energy. When hungry we have less energy.
Where do animals get energy? What do cars and scooters ...: Animals from food. Vehicles need petrol or diesel.
imp_items: What does energy do? Name one thing.
It makes things move, light, sound or heat
Name four things that need energy and what they do.
Fan moves; bulb lights; bell sounds; stove heats
Why do we feel tired when hungry?
Food gives energy to the body
Name two fuels.
Petrol and diesel
Write two problems of burning wood and coal.
Smoke makes the air dirty and trees are cut
Name two ways electricity helps us.
It gives light and runs machines

subject: EVS
title: Clothes — How Things are Made
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 8, Clothes — How Things are Made, the topics are: Weaving — Over and Under, handloom and textile mills — weaving traditions of india, spinning — making thread from fibres, natural and synthetic fibres, silk and the life cycle of the silk moth, stitching — joining cloth with needle and thread (running stitch), embroidery — stitches that decorate, reuse and recycle old clothes. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Weaving — Over and Under
Weaving crosses two sets of threads or strips — one going up and down, the other going across — over and under each other, to ...
Handloom and Textile Mills — Weaving Traditions of India
People in India have woven cloth for 4,000 years
Spinning — Making Thread from Fibres
Thread (yarn) is made by twisting fibres together — this is spinning
Natural and Synthetic Fibres
Fibres come from natural sources (bamboo, cotton, linen, wool, silk, jute) or are made by humans from artificial materials ...
Silk and the Life Cycle of the Silk Moth
Silk is a natural fibre from the cocoon of the silk moth
Stitching — Joining Cloth with Needle and Thread (Running Stitch)
Stitching joins pieces together with a needle and thread
Embroidery — Stitches that Decorate
Stitches do not only join cloth — they also decorate it
Reuse and Recycle Old Clothes
In India people rarely throw clothes: they hand them down, remake them into something else, or join small pieces into quilts

items: Weaving crosses two sets of threads or strips — one going up and down, the other going across — over and under each other, to make one strong fabric like a mat, a basket or cloth.
Weaving = two sets of threads crossed over and under
Paper strips → mat; threads → cloth
Every cloth shows a criss-cross pattern

notes.h: Handloom and Textile Mills — Weaving Traditions of India
items: People in India have woven cloth for 4,000 years. Cloth woven by hand on a loom is handloom fabric; textile mills weave with machines in large amounts. Handloom traditions give work to families and keep skills alive.
Loom = instrument for weaving by hand
Handloom fabric = woven by hand on a loom
Mills = machines, large quantities
Gujarat: Patola, Ikat, Kala cotton
Thread (yarn) is made by twisting fibres together — this is spinning. A charkha spins thread from cotton. Untwist a thread and you find thin hair-like fibres.
India was the first country to grow cotton and use it to make clothes
Fibres → twist (spin) → thread
Twisting makes the strand stronger
Fibres come from natural sources (bamboo, cotton, linen, wool, silk, jute) or are made by humans from artificial materials (nylon, rayon, polyester, terylene). We use both.
Natural: bamboo, cotton, linen, wool, silk, jute
Synthetic: nylon, rayon, polyester, terylene
We use both

notes.h: Silk and the Life Cycle of the Silk Moth
items: Silk is a natural fibre from the cocoon of the silk moth. Cocoons are put in hot water and the silk thread is pulled out. The moth grows in a life cycle: eggs → caterpillar → cocoon → moth, and again.
Silk = from the cocoon of the silk moth
Eggs → caterpillar → cocoon → moth → eggs
Caterpillars eat mulberry leaves

notes.h: Stitching — Joining Cloth with Needle and Thread (Running Stitch)
items: Stitching joins pieces together with a needle and thread. The simplest stitch is the running stitch — up, down, up, down in a straight line. One thread runs through all the stitches, so each thread matters.
Needle + thread join cloth
Running stitch: up, down in a straight line
Each thread is important
Stitches do not only join cloth — they also decorate it. Each region of India has its own embroidery, which tells the story of its place and people.
Stitches join AND decorate
8 embroideries, each from its own place
Rajasthan has two: Banjara and Gota
In India people rarely throw clothes: they hand them down, remake them into something else, or join small pieces into quilts. Every cloth took fibres, spinning, weaving and stitching to make.
Hand down · remake · quilt
Making cloth takes a lot of work and material — so do not waste it
Reusing means less waste
Wrong: Cloth is one smooth sheet, like paper. Right: Cloth is many tiny threads crossed over and under — see the criss-cross under a magnifying glass
Wrong: All cloth today is made in mills; handloom is gone. Right: Handloom still gives work to over 45 lakh people
Wrong: Thread grows ready-made on the cotton plant. Right: Cotton gives fibres; they must be twisted (spun) into thread
Wrong: All fibres come from cotton. Right: Bamboo, linen, jute, wool and silk are natural fibres too
Wrong: Silk is made in a factory from chemicals. Right: Silk is natural — it comes from the cocoon of the silk moth
Wrong: If one thread breaks, only that one stitch is lost. Right: The same thread runs through all the stitches, so the stitching can open up

sol_items: What do you see in the picture of nests?: Weaver bird nests hanging from a branch.
Which hidden artist has woven long before humans?: The weaver bird (and spiders).
Things woven from natural materials at home: Baskets, mats and bags.
Can you make a basket by over-under weaving?: Yes. Cross strips over one and under the next.
Woven things in the classroom: Uniform cloth, bag and a mat.
Cloth under a magnifying glass: Yes, we see a criss-cross pattern of threads.
imp_items: What is weaving?
Crossing threads over and under each other
What is a handloom?
A loom worked by hand
What is spinning?
Twisting fibres to make thread
What spins cotton into thread?
A charkha
Name two natural and two synthetic fibres.
Natural: cotton, silk; synthetic: nylon, polyester
Write the life cycle of the silk moth.
Egg, larva, cocoon, moth

subject: EVS
title: Rhythms of Nature
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 9, Rhythms of Nature, the topics are: Changes Around Us, day and night, seasons' chart: tracking changes in a year, discovering seasons: the six seasons of india, celebrating seasons: crops, festivals and our lives. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Changes Around Us
We and everything around us keep changing
Day and Night
Day and night happen because the Earth rotates (spins)
Seasons' Chart: Tracking Changes in a Year
By writing what we observe in a seasons' journal all year and putting everyone's notes on one class chart — 5 themes × 4 time ...
Discovering Seasons: The Six Seasons of India
The changes of the year follow a pattern that repeats every year — this repeating pattern in nature is called seasons
Celebrating Seasons: Crops, Festivals and Our Lives
Seasons shape our lives: farmers grow different crops in different seasons, many festivals are linked to seasons, and what we ...

items: We and everything around us keep changing. Some changes take years, some take days, some only minutes or seconds — and some changes come back again and again, like a rhythm.
Changes happen all the time — to us and around us.
Changes take different times: years, days, minutes, seconds.
Changes that repeat again and again are the rhythms of nature.

Day and night happen because the Earth rotates (spins). The side of the Earth facing the Sun has day; the side away from the Sun has night. The Sun stays in one place — it only seems to rise in the east and set in the west.
The Earth rotates; the Sun stays in one place.
Side facing the Sun = day; side away = night.
The Sun only seems to rise in the east and set in the west.

notes.h: Seasons' Chart: Tracking Changes in a Year
items: By writing what we observe in a seasons' journal all year and putting everyone's notes on one class chart — 5 themes × 4 time periods — we can see how nature and people change through the year.
Journal first: note what you see all year.
Chart: 5 themes in rows, 4 time periods in columns.
Read a row → how one theme changes in the year; read a column → everything in one period.

notes.h: Discovering Seasons: The Six Seasons of India
items: The changes of the year follow a pattern that repeats every year — this repeating pattern in nature is called seasons. India has six seasons, and the same season feels different in different places.
Seasons = the repeating pattern of change every year.
Six seasons: Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemant, Shishir.
The same season can be very different in different places.

notes.h: Celebrating Seasons: Crops, Festivals and Our Lives
items: Seasons shape our lives: farmers grow different crops in different seasons, many festivals are linked to seasons, and what we eat, wear and sing changes with them. Seasons show that life moves in cycles and change is natural and necessary.
Seasons are not just weather — they shape crops, food, clothes and festivals.
Seasons teach that life moves in cycles.
Change is natural and necessary.
Wrong: All changes take a long time. Right: Some take years, but some happen in days, minutes or even seconds
Wrong: The Sun moves around and goes down under the Earth at night. Right: The Sun stays in one place; the Earth rotates, so we turn away from the Sun
Wrong: Only plants change through the year. Right: Animals, air, heat and light, water and people's activities change too — that is why the chart has five themes
Wrong: India has only three seasons: summer, monsoon and winter. Right: These are the three big ones, but India has six seasons, each lasting about two months
Wrong: Any crop can be grown in any season. Right: Some crops grow best in winter, some in summer heat, and some need the rainy season's water

sol_items: Something that changes over years; in a few years; ever...: Mountains wear down over years; a sapling becomes a tree in a few years; seasons come every year; ice melts in minutes.
What causes day and night? Is the Sun moving?: The Earth spins, so the side facing the Sun has day. The Sun only seems to move.
Globe and light demonstration: Light falls on one side (day) and the other side is dark (night).
When it is day in India, which countries have nigh: Countries on the far side of the Earth, such as the USA (read from the globe).
Did the same changes happen last year? Will they n: Yes. Seasonal changes repeat every year.
Names of seasons in your region; how many in India: Six: spring, summer, monsoon, autumn, pre-winter and winter (names vary by language).
imp_items: Name something that changes every year.
Seasons
Give examples of changes that take long, a few years and a few minutes.
Mountain: long; sapling to tree: few years; ice melting: minutes
What causes day and night?
Earth spins; the side facing the Sun has day
Does the Sun move around the Earth?
No; it only seems to move
When it is day in India where may it be night?
On the far side of Earth, such as the USA
How many seasons are there in India?
Six

subject: EVS
title: Earth — Our Shared Home
intro: In Class 5 EVS Chapter 10, Earth — Our Shared Home, the topics are: Earth, the Blue Planet, rosy starlings — nature has no boundaries, chilli — from south america to india, marigold — from mexico to india, yoga — india's gift to the world, sugar — india's sweet gift, indian cows in brazil, web of life — we are all connected, one earth, one family — vasudhaiva kutumbakam. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Earth, the Blue Planet
Seen from space, Earth is one blue planet of land and sea, with no borders between countries
Rosy Starlings — Nature Has No Boundaries
Nature has no boundaries: air, water, clouds, seeds and animals move freely across the world
Chilli — From South America to India
Chilli plants once grew only in South America
Marigold — From Mexico to India
The marigold flower is from Mexico, where it is used in festivals
Yoga — India's Gift to the World
Yoga has been practised in India for more than 3,000 years to keep the body healthy and the mind peaceful
Sugar — India's Sweet Gift
Long ago people elsewhere did not know sugar and used honey
Indian Cows in Brazil
Long ago Portuguese traders took some Indian cows to Brazil
Web of Life — We Are All Connected
The stories are not only about birds, plants or objects — they are about people, journeys, sharing and the blending of cultures
One Earth, One Family — Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' — the world is one family

items: Seen from space, Earth is one blue planet of land and sea, with no borders between countries. All of us live on it — every address on Earth ends with the same planet.
From space: one Earth, no borders.
Every address ends with Planet Earth.
All oceans are connected.

notes.h: Rosy Starlings — Nature Has No Boundaries
items: Nature has no boundaries: air, water, clouds, seeds and animals move freely across the world. Rosy starlings fly thousands of kilometres every winter from southern Russia and Mongolia to India, enjoy the warm weather and eat crop pests.
Rosy starlings: Russia, Mongolia → India every winter.
They eat locusts and grasshoppers.
Nature has no boundaries.

notes.h: Chilli — From South America to India
items: Chilli plants once grew only in South America. 400 to 500 years ago travellers from Portugal brought them to India, where they found new soil and climate and entered our kitchens. Before chilli, Indian food was spiced with black pepper.
Chilli: South America → India.
Brought by travellers from Portugal, 400–500 years ago.
Before chilli: black pepper.

The marigold flower is from Mexico, where it is used in festivals. It travelled across the world to India and found a new home; its bright orange and yellow colours fit our sense of warmth, celebration and spirituality.
Marigold: Mexico → India.
Used in festivals in both lands.
Bright orange and yellow = warmth and celebration.

notes.h: Yoga — India's Gift to the World
items: Yoga has been practised in India for more than 3,000 years to keep the body healthy and the mind peaceful. Travellers, scholars and teachers from India shared it, and today it is practised in almost every country.
Yoga: India → the world.
3,000+ years old.
21 June: International Day of Yoga (UN, 2014).

Long ago people elsewhere did not know sugar and used honey. The method of making jaggery from sugarcane juice was first discovered in India, then jaggery was made into sugar; this knowledge spread to the world through trade and travel.
Sugarcane juice → jaggery → sugar (India first).
Spread by trade and travel.
Rice, mangoes, bananas also went from India.

Long ago Portuguese traders took some Indian cows to Brazil. They were strong, gave good milk and did not mind Brazil's weather, so they grew in number; today more than three-fourths of Brazil's milk comes from three Indian breeds — Gir, Kankrej and Ongole.
Indian cows → Brazil, by Portuguese traders.
Strong, good milk, suit the weather.
Gir, Kankrej, Ongole: over 3/4 of Brazil's milk.

notes.h: Web of Life — We Are All Connected
items: The stories are not only about birds, plants or objects — they are about people, journeys, sharing and the blending of cultures. Earth is a living web of life where people, animals, plants and ideas travel, mix and grow together; by learning, sharing and caring we become part of it.
Journeys go both ways.
People, animals, plants and ideas travel, mix and grow together.
We are all connected — a web of life.

notes.h: One Earth, One Family — Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
items: 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' — the world is one family. All people, animals, trees, rivers, air and sky belong to it; we live together, depend on each other and share one Earth. Earth is the only planet we know with life, so caring for it means caring for each other.
Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam = the world is one family.
Earth: only planet we know with life.
Caring for Earth = caring for each other.
Wrong: From space you can see the lines between countries, like on a map. Right: Border lines are drawn only on maps; from space Earth looks completely one
Wrong: Borders between countries stop birds and clouds. Right: Nature has no boundaries — birds, air, water, clouds and seeds move freely
Wrong: Chilli has always grown in India. Right: Chilli came from South America; travellers from Portugal brought it 400–500 years ago
Wrong: The marigold first grew in India. Right: The marigold is from Mexico; it travelled to India and found a new home
Wrong: Yoga is a new exercise from other countries. Right: Yoga began in India and has been practised here for more than 3,000 years
Wrong: Sugar came to India from other countries. Right: Sugar travelled FROM India — jaggery and sugar making were first discovered here

sol_items: Are all oceans connected? Where is India?: Yes, all oceans are connected. India is in Asia (read from the globe).
What does the rosy starling story tell us?: Birds fly across countries, so nature has no boundaries.
Birds that visit in winter; trace the path; postca: They come from places like Russia and Mongolia. Wind and warm weather help the journey.
What does "nature has no boundaries" mean?: Air, water, seeds and animals move freely across countries.
What if chillies disappeared for a week? Recipe with bl...: Food would taste less hot. Pepper rasam is a recipe.
Journey of chillies; potato, tomato, peanut or cas: Chillies came from South America with Portuguese travellers. Potato and tomato also came from the Americas.
